definition: Cross-cultural psychology is the study of how cultural traditions, knowledge structures, and values shape psychological processes and their interpretation. In this context, it is used to explain why theories built mainly from one cultural tradition may need to be extended to account for culturally specific patterns of perception, emotion, and meaning.

reasons: The packet does not provide a general definition of “cross-cultural psychology” as a field (“the study of…”)—it only mentions cross-cultural psychology as part of an integrative framework for a specific neuroaesthetics/theoretical-extension project.

The definition’s claims about culture shaping psychological processes and their interpretation, and about extending theories more broadly beyond one cultural tradition, are only indirectly reflected in the packet’s description of extending European-based aesthetic models to traditional Chinese contexts, not stated as the definition of the term itself.

The packet uses “cross-cultural psychology” to motivate culturally pluralistic extension in neuroaesthetics; it does not support the definition’s broader scope statement that cultural traditions/values shape psychological processes across the field.
The packet does not define cross-cultural psychology as a general field or as the study of how cultural traditions, knowledge structures, and values shape psychological processes and interpretation.

The packet supports only a specific application in a neuroaesthetics framework: culturally specific mechanisms, cultural mediation, and culturally specific knowledge structures in Chinese aesthetic processing. It does not support the broader explanatory claim that theories from one cultural tradition need to be extended to account for culturally specific patterns of perception, emotion, and meaning as a general definition of the term.
